olm8ij-d1e1723.summary: Aureol's commentary on Book II, Distinction 44, the last distinction of Book II, follows Lombard's two themes: the power to sin, and secular power and obedience. A short preamble announces four questions, which are treated as four articles of a single quaestio. The first two give a theory of peccability. The power to sin is not free choice as such, nor limitation, nor being from nothing, since the Virgin, the confirmed and the blessed have all three and cannot sin. It is free choice insofar as it is neither the first rule of rectitude nor of itself conformed to that rule. Only the divine will is that rule, so whatever God commands is right. Grace, as charity conforming the created will to God's, is the sole source of creaturely impeccability. Everything intrinsic to the power to sin is from God, since defect enters only connotatively, as its object. The last two articles form a compact political theory. Power and lordship are relations of reason, yet right reason requires rule, for directing and coercing, even in the state of innocence. It favours a single monarch or an ordered hierarchy of monarchies, licenses the deposition of incorrigible tyrants and the just subjection of lawless nations (explaining Roman imperial rule), and sees universal monarchies as disposed by God and lesser principalities as permitted. Obedience, owed to law as well as to princes, is a special moral virtue under justice. The distinction closes Book II with a doxology.
claims: The power to sin is founded in a free will that is neither the first rule nor of itself conformed to it.
The divine will is the first rule of rectitude; grace alone makes the created will impeccable.
Everything intrinsic to the power to sin is from God; defect is only connoted.
Power and lordship are relations of reason, yet rule among humans is required by right reason.
Right reason favours universal monarchy, and universal monarchies are disposed by God.
Obedience is a special moral virtue under justice, owed to law as well as to rulers.

olm8ij-bb3200.summary: Aureol's commentary on Book III, Distinction 23 has four questions that move from Christology to moral psychology and the theory of virtue. Q1 asks whether a divine person could assume a man without quantity. Aureol answers yes, distinguishing man as a natural being, whose definition includes quantity, from man as a metaphysical being of matter and substantial form. Such a man would keep a natural inclination to quantity. An accident can depend on a sustaining cause without informing it, as in the Eucharist. Q2 asks whether the irascible and concupiscible are distinct powers. After rejecting five accounts, Aureol holds that irascible acts are formally a rising up or straining toward the arduous, meaning what is attainable with difficulty, and always presuppose a concupiscible act. They are distinct powers in both the sensitive and the rational appetite, against an 'ancient doctor' and Henry of Ghent, but less distinct in the will. Q3 asks what a moral habit adds to a power. Six experienced marks of the virtuous (facility, readiness, firmness, steadiness, delight, promptness) argue a real addition that inclines the power like a weight. That addition is neither a relation nor a separable thing but a mode, a disposition 'of this toward that' in the first species of quality. Q4 asks about the source of virtue. True virtue simply taken requires divine acceptance and infused virtue, while pagans can have virtue in a human mode. Habits come from acts. Complexion-based natural dispositions are not virtues and never become virtues, though they dispose to them. Hope is formally a spiritual rising toward an arduous good, and is an infused theological virtue whose formal object is God and material object beatitude. Questions 2 to 4 are connected: the theory of rising (assurrectio) worked out for the irascible in Q2 grounds the account of hope in Q4, and Q3's experiential marks of habit are invoked again in Q4.
claims: A divine person could assume a man without quantity, considered metaphysically.
Irascible acts are formally a rising toward the arduous; irascible and concupiscible are distinct powers in both appetites.
A virtuous habit is a real mode of the power, a disposition 'of this toward that' in the first species of quality.
True virtue simply taken requires divine acceptance; natural dispositions are not virtues.
Hope is a spiritual rising toward an arduous good and an infused theological virtue with God as formal object.

olm8ij-d1e66.summary: Partial summary of Book II of Aureol's Sentences commentary, based only on Distinction 44, the one distinction of Book II interpreted so far (1 of 44 direct children). It does not represent the rest of Book II. Distinction 44, the last of the book, argues that the power to sin lies in a free will that is neither the first rule of rectitude nor of itself conformed to it. Only grace makes a creature impeccable, and everything intrinsic to the power to sin is from God. It then sets out a political theory: power is a relation of reason, rule is required by right reason, a single monarch or an ordered hierarchy of monarchies is favoured, and tyrants may be resisted. Obedience is treated as a special moral virtue under justice. The book closes with a doxology.
claims: (From d.44 only) The power to sin is founded in a free will that is not the first rule of rectitude.
(From d.44 only) Right reason requires rule among humans and favours universal monarchy.
(From d.44 only) Obedience is a special moral virtue under justice.

olm8ij-bb2710.summary: Partial summary of Book III of Aureol's Sentences commentary, based only on Distinction 23, the one distinction of Book III interpreted so far (1 of 28 direct children). It does not represent Book III's treatment of the Incarnation as a whole. Distinction 23 holds that a divine person could assume a man without quantity, considered metaphysically. It argues that the irascible and concupiscible are distinct powers in both appetites, irascible acts being a rising toward the arduous. It analyses a moral habit as a real mode of the power, a disposition 'of this toward that' in the first species of quality. Finally, it distinguishes true virtue, which requires divine acceptance and infusion, from naturally acquired virtue in a human mode, and treats hope as an infused theological virtue whose formal object is God.
claims: (From d.23 only) A divine person could assume a man without quantity.
(From d.23 only) Irascible and concupiscible are distinct powers in both appetites.
(From d.23 only) A virtuous habit is a mode of the power in the first species of quality.
(From d.23 only) Hope is an infused theological virtue with God as formal object.

olm8ij.summary: Partial summary of Peter Auriol's Commentarius in Libros Sententiarum as encoded in this repository (Books II, III and IV). It rests only on the partial summaries of Book II (from Distinction 44 alone) and Book III (from Distinction 23 alone). Book IV has no interpretations yet (2 of 3 direct children covered, both of them partial). In these two distinctions Auriol works across moral theology, political theory, Christology and psychology. Several commitments recur. Rectitude is measured ultimately by the divine will, the first rule; true virtue simply taken requires divine acceptance and grace; and naturally acquired virtue conforms only to right reason. Auriol often argues from inner experience, as in the experienced marks of habit, the experience of inclination, and the separability of hope from desire. He distinguishes modes from things and dispositions from relations: power is a relation of reason, while habit is a mode of the power. And he attends to the 'rising' (assurrectio) of the irascible, which grounds his account of hope. These are features of the interpreted portions only.
claims: (From II d.44 and III d.23 only) The divine will is the first rule of rectitude, and grace alone secures impeccability and simply true virtue.
(From II d.44 and III d.23 only) Political power is a relation of reason, while a virtuous habit is a real mode of the power.
(From II d.44 and III d.23 only) Irascible acts, including hope, are formally a rising toward an arduous good.
